gen_risks.description: Escalating insecurity and conflict may restrict access to target areas, delaying or halting project activities.
gen_risks.mitigation: Implement security SOPs, use remote delivery tools, partner with NGOs that have field access, and activate contingency plans for suspension if needed.
gen_risks.evidence: Annex 3 security risk matrix describing green/yellow/red risk levels and adaptations for economic inclusion and registry activities.

gen_risks.description: Procurement delays caused by administrative routines and limited competition in fragile areas could affect timely delivery of goods and services.
gen_risks.mitigation: Recruit a qualified procurement specialist, develop a detailed procurement procedures section in the PIM, and conduct fast‑track procurement trainings for DMP, DCMEF and bid committees.
gen_risks.evidence: Procurement risk assessment notes administrative routines may cause delays; limited bidders in fragile areas (section 83‑85).

gen_risks.description: The newly created PIU lacks experienced financial management staff and systems, increasing fiduciary risk.
gen_risks.mitigation: Recruit qualified FM staff by effectiveness, install approved accounting software, adopt a comprehensive FM manual, and engage an external auditor and internal audit arrangements.
gen_risks.evidence: FM assessment finds PIU has no FM staff, procedures, software; mitigation measures listed (section 82).

gen_risks.description: Sexual exploitation, abuse and harassment (SEA/SH) incidents could arise among vulnerable beneficiaries, especially women and IDPs.
gen_risks.mitigation: Implement an SEA/SH Action Plan with community sensitisation, a grievance mechanism, referral pathways to GBV services, and train all staff on code of conduct.
gen_risks.evidence: SEA/SH risk classified as Substantial; mitigation via Action Plan and Grievance Mechanism (section 87‑88).

gen_risks.description: Construction of warehouses and logistics infrastructure may cause water and soil pollution.
gen_risks.mitigation: Apply ESS 3 (pollution prevention) standards, conduct site‑specific environmental management plans, and monitor waste handling during construction.
gen_risks.evidence: E&S risks include water and soil pollution from construction sites (section 87).

gen_risks.description: Interoperability of the RSU with other databases may breach data protection regulations, exposing personal data.
gen_risks.mitigation: Engage the National Data Protection Authority to review data sharing protocols, implement encryption and access controls, and conduct privacy impact assessments.
gen_risks.evidence: Interoperability work will follow national data protection authority guidance (section 34‑35).

gen_risks.description: Complex coordination among multiple ministries and partners could lead to fragmented implementation and duplication.
gen_risks.mitigation: Establish a formal inter‑ministerial coordination unit, define clear roles in the PIM, and hold regular joint planning meetings.
gen_risks.evidence: Section 58‑59 notes fragmentation and need for stronger coordination mechanisms.

gen_risks.description: Severe climate events (droughts, floods) may disrupt beneficiary participation and damage project assets.
gen_risks.mitigation: Integrate climate‑resilient livelihood packages, use early warning systems for shock‑responsive targeting, and design warehouses to withstand extreme weather.
gen_risks.evidence: Strategic context describes climate shocks and adaptation measures (section 2‑3, 77).

gen_risks.description: Declining humanitarian funding could reduce complementary support for IDPs, affecting project outcomes.
gen_risks.mitigation: Secure additional development financing through private sector partnerships, and build contingency buffers in the project budget for IDP‑specific activities.
gen_risks.evidence: Section 6 notes reduced humanitarian funding since 2025 and increased national ownership.

gen_risks.description: Delay in recruiting key PIU staff (GBV specialist, security specialist, external auditor) may hinder compliance with legal covenants.
gen_risks.mitigation: Set firm recruitment timelines in the PIM, use competitive hiring processes, and monitor progress through quarterly PIU reports.
gen_risks.evidence: Legal covenants require recruitment within 3‑6 months after effectiveness (section FA Schedule 2).

gen_risks.description: Women may face barriers to opening bank accounts (KYC) limiting financial inclusion benefits.
gen_risks.mitigation: Partner with MFIs to simplify KYC procedures, provide ID document assistance, and offer mobile‑money alternatives where banking is limited.
gen_risks.evidence: Component 1.1 mentions gender‑sensitive adaptations such as daycare and KYC support (section 24‑25).

gen_risks.description: Certain vulnerable groups (people with disabilities, elderly) may be excluded from RSU registration and benefits.
gen_risks.mitigation: Include explicit inclusion criteria in the proxy means test, conduct outreach through disability NGOs, and monitor disaggregated registration data.
gen_risks.evidence: RSU aims to cover female‑headed households, displaced persons, persons with disability (section 32).

gen_risks.description: Fraud or corruption in procurement could undermine project credibility and financial integrity.
gen_risks.mitigation: Apply World Bank anti‑corruption guidelines, conduct regular audits by ASCELC, and use FundsChain for real‑time tracking of disbursements.
gen_risks.evidence: Procurement risk includes fraud; fiduciary controls described in disbursement arrangements (section 70‑71).

gen_risks.description: Security constraints may limit field monitoring, reducing data quality for M&E.
gen_risks.mitigation: Utilise remote monitoring tools (GEMS, phone‑based PDM, IBM), and schedule periodic third‑party verification missions in accessible zones.
gen_risks.evidence: Monitoring plan mentions remote tools for insecure areas (section 67‑68, Annex 3).

gen_risks.description: Roll‑out of the Unique Social Registry may be slower than planned, limiting beneficiary targeting.
gen_risks.mitigation: Set phased rollout milestones, allocate dedicated staff for data collection, and monitor progress against a detailed implementation schedule.
gen_risks.evidence: RSU rollout targets 800,000 households; timeline described in Subcomponent 2.1 (section 32‑33).

gen_risks.description: Failure to achieve system interoperability could result in duplicate beneficiary records and inefficient service delivery.
gen_risks.mitigation: Develop a clear interoperability architecture, conduct regular data reconciliation tests, and enforce standardized data exchange protocols.
gen_risks.evidence: Subcomponent 2.2 outlines need for interoperable framework and data exchange (section 34‑36).

gt_risks.description: Political and governance risk is assessed to be Substantial. The uncertain political and governance context provides a challenge to long-term development policy. Adaptive social protection systems are still nascent and will require continued political commitment.
gt_risks.mitigation: The team, guided by the management, will continue its high-level policy dialogue at central and decentralized levels and ensure continuous advocacy and communication.

gt_risks.description: Macroeconomic risk is assessed to be Substantial. Fiscal space remains constrained by elevated security spending and tighter financing conditions, which increase the risk of reduced budget allocations and delayed counterpart funding for new priorities and reforms, including social protection and the PAMPV. Macroeconomic risks also arise from exogenous factors, including current conflict in the Middle East which can result in a surge in oil prices and put inflationary pressure.
gt_risks.mitigation: Other programs such as the International Monetary Fund program and the World Bank's technical assistance on tax expenditure under the Sustainable Development Finance Policy can help expand fiscal space, partially mitigating these risks.

gt_risks.description: Sector strategy and policies risks are considered to be Substantial. Sectoral strategies and policies remain nascent, and the Government's budget allocation to operationalize the PAMPV remains unclear. Also, sectoral decisions are at times taken abruptly and can heavily affect implementation (for example, the suspension of cash transfers in 2023 led to an increased focus on economic inclusion, and the newly emerged priority of the CONASUR/IDPs led to the revision of the fiche de projet of this project).
gt_risks.mitigation: In parallel with high-level policy dialogue, the project supports strategic communications, adopts an agile approach, and provides technical assistance to promote evidence-based decision-making (with support from SASPP, the Social Protection Response MDTF, and the State and Peacebuilding Fund).

gt_risks.description: Overall fiduciary risks are considered as Substantial, as described in section IV.B and annex 2, based on financial assessment and procurement assessment.
gt_risks.mitigation: The project preparation fund (Grant Facility for Project Preparation) has been used not only to prepare mitigation measures to address these risks but will also elevate the project readiness (for example, effectiveness-linked actions including FM and procurement staffing and initiating the procurement packages for the first 18-months' implementation priorities) to improve the project performance.

gt_risks.description: Other risks related to insecurity are rated as High. The deteriorating and volatile security situation—particularly in regions with high poverty, displacement, and food insecurity that are project intervention areas—will likely be an important risk. The project will also address other risks related to protection of personal data: for Component 2 on social registry and interoperability, activities will be guided by the Information System Security Policy (ISSP) document developed by the ANSSI, to ensure confidentiality of households registered in the RSU.
gt_risks.mitigation: The project activities will be adjusted based on the security situation (see annex 3), and the PIU will be also staffed with a security specialist and a security management plan will be developed. To remain engaged, the project will also rely on remote delivery/monitoring, partnering with local representation (NGOs, UN agencies). The ST-RSU will conduct capacity-building activities, including training sessions and awareness campaigns, to strengthen users' ability to manage and protect households' personal data.
